newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee plummets as supply woes start to ease.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee plummets as supply woes start to ease.

text.p: Continued speculative profit-taking pushed CSCE coffee prices sharply lower for the second consecutive session on Thursday amid a slight easing of supply concerns, market sources said.

The most-active May contract plummeted 13.85 cents per lb -- or seven percent, to close at 182.25 cents, after ranging between 194.60 and 181.00. Spot March dropped 13.65 cents, to 202.00 cents, while the rest finished 11.75 to 14.50 lower.
"The fundamentals are slowly changing," said Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka. "Higher prices for coffee will bring more coffee into the market."
"Colombia is selling old-crop coffee to make money," he added. "Brazil is selling old-crop coffee to make money."
Spilka said data released earlier this week by the Brazilian Federation of Coffee Exporters (FEBEC) illustrated origins' efforts to take advantage of the market's recent surge in prices.
FEBEC said Brazilian coffee exports so far this year have reached 2.33 million bags, nearly twice the 1.18 million bags shipped in the first two months of 1996.
The recent buildup in certified stocks also showed more coffee was finding its way to the market, Spilka said.

After Thursday's close, the CSCE reported certified coffee stocks grew for the sixth day in a row, reaching 42,333 60-kg bags as of March 12. There were an additional 18,446 bags pending grading, the exchange said.

Since early December, the price of coffee futures has nearly doubled on worries about short supplies. Low stock levels in both consuming and producing nations, coupled with projections for smaller crops in many Latin American countries, fueled supply woes.

But after virtually running straight up, many traders and analysts said the market's latest setback was inevitable. However, continued uncertainty about the size of crops in top producers Brazil and Colombia should keep the market underpinned, they said.
Technically, floor traders said the active May contract's failure to get past near-term resistance at 205.50 cents on Monday and Tuesday weighed on the market from the outset on Wednesday.

Brushing aside its opening call, prices headed into negative territory and remained there the entire day. Traders said downward momentum accelerated after the key May contract fell through support at 190.00 cents per lb and touched off a series of commission house sell-stops below that level.
Today's close below Monday's low of 185.20 cents basis May is likely to dampen chartists' enthusiasm, traders said. A chart gap between 177.00 and 175.50 was seen as May support, they said.
Today's turnover was estimated at 12,759 lots, compared with Wednesday's official tally of 10,761 lots. ((--Patricia Avidan, New York Commodity Desk +1 212 859 1640))
